title: Humility that raises
hookLine: one hadith promises that the way up runs downward

lines: HUMBLED FOR ALLAH, RAISED BY ALLAH.
cards: Where do you sit when you walk into a crowded room? Near the front, where you'll be seen? By the door, where you can slip out?
Or wherever's left? One hadith turns the whole question upside down.

In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah, except that Allah raises him. The way up runs downward. Today's word: tawadu', humility.

teach.h: FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH, NOT FOR SHOW.
teach.b: Notice the small phrase in the middle: for the sake of Allah. This isn't putting yourself down to be noticed, or false modesty fishing for a compliment.
It's lowering yourself where Allah sees it, and leaving the raising to Him. The hadith doesn't say how or when. Only who does it.
The Qur'an draws the same posture as a way of walking.
Surah al-Furqan, in Pickthall's translation: "The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace."
Humility in the feet, and in the reply when someone is rude. Then why it matters between people.

teach.h: NO ONE BOASTS, NO ONE WRONGS.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet said Allah revealed to him: be humble toward one another, so that no one boasts over another, and no one wrongs another.
Pride isn't only a private flaw; it's where boasting and wronging start. And in a life? Someone asked 'A'ishah what he did at home.

teach.h: IN THE SERVICE OF HIS FAMILY.
teach.b: Her answer, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: he was in the service of his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray.
And Anas reports, also in Bukhari, that any slave girl of Medina could take the Prophet by the hand and lead him wherever she needed. So tawadu' isn't a mood of feeling small.
It's a set of movements: the lower seat, the soft step, the chores at home, the hand that lets itself be taken.

how: Muslim teaching on tawadu' draws on Qur'an 25:63 and the hadith that no one humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him, and on reports of the Prophet serving his family at home.

o: putting yourself down so others will praise your modesty
the quiet calm of a person who never feels any pride
humility: lowering yourself for Allah, who does the raising

p: in the service of his family
could lead him by the hand

s: the hadith praises putting yourself down so others notice
the lowering is for the sake of Allah, and the raising is left to Him.
al-Furqan pairs humble walking with answering the foolish: Peace
they walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish address them, answer: Peace.
the Prophet left household work to others
'A'ishah said he was in the service of his family until prayer time (Bukhari).

games.q: someone asks 'A'ishah what the Prophet did at home. what does she say?
o: he was in the service of his family, then went out to pray.
games.why: he served his family, and when prayer came, he went out to pray (Bukhari).

practice: Picture one place you'll sit today, a meeting, a table, a bus, and in your mind take the lower seat there, letting someone else have the better chair, the first word, the credit.
Notice what pulls at you without arguing with it, then see yourself quietly doing one chore you usually leave to someone else. If you pray, you can make that small lowering for the sake of Allah.

wordCard.voice: Tawadu'. Humility: lowering yourself for the sake of Allah, in your seat, your step and your service, and leaving the raising to Him. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: lowered, raised. You do the lowering; the raising is left to Him. See you tomorrow.
